title: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome: Diagnosis, pathophysiology, and treatment—A systematic review

claims.statement: In published cases of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, again and again, in people who use cannabis regularly), pooled descriptively in a systematic review of reports from 2000 to September 2015 (Sorensen et al., 2017; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 211 patients from 80 case reports and 7 case series, 98 of them from one series entered as summary figures; no randomized trials, no comparison groups and no count of how many people who use cannabis develop the syndrome), all patients had recurrent vomiting with severe nausea and 85.1% had abdominal pain; 154 of 211 (72.9%) were men; the median age was 16 at first cannabis use (IQR 14 to 18; 84 patients), 24 at the start of symptoms (19 to 29; 101) and 28 at diagnosis (22 to 34; 111). Of the 197 whose frequency of use was reported, 76.6% used cannabis daily or more often and 97.4% at least weekly, and 45 of 179 (25.1%) had used for a year or less before symptoms began. Of the patients whose bathing was reported, 157 of 170 (92.3%) found that hot baths or showers relieved their symptoms. Of the 64 patients whose stopping was documented, 62 (96.8%) had complete resolution of symptoms; the two without resolution had no urine test to confirm that they had stopped, and all 21 patients who kept using still had symptoms. Follow-up was documented for only 85 of the 211 patients (40.2%), no time to resolution is reported, and whether symptoms returned when people started again was too inconsistently documented to count. The review proposes recognising the syndrome by severe cyclic vomiting, usually with abdominal pain, at least weekly cannabis use before symptoms began, temporary relief with hot bathing and resolution after stopping, with male sex, starting cannabis in the teenage years and symptoms beginning in the twenties as supporting features; these features come from cases diagnosed by them, so their frequencies do not show how well they separate the syndrome from other causes of repeated vomiting, which no study in the review tested. Diagnosis came on average 4.1 years (SD 4.6) after symptoms began, and in four case reports patients were first diagnosed with severe vomiting of pregnancy. A 2021 review says the distinction from other cyclic vomiting disorders is underdeveloped and cites two sources for 90% of patients reporting that hot baths and stopping cannabis relieve their symptoms (Connor et al., 2021; second-hand), and a 2014 review links repeated use with increased vomiting without a citation (Volkow et al., 2014). All nine proposed mechanisms were rated very low, and three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids; acute hospital treatments are covered in the claims on capsaicin cream and on dopamine-blocking medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Sorensen 2017 cumulative synthesis (211 patients; each share is of the patients in whom the feature was reported): recurrent vomiting 100% (211); severe nausea and vomiting 100% (211); abdominal pain 85.1% (202); relief with hot bathing 92.3% (157 of 170); resolution after stopping 96.8% (62 of 64; all 21 who kept using had ongoing symptoms); at least weekly use 97.4% (197); daily or more 76.6% (197); regular use for more than a year 74.8% (179); men 72.9% (154 of 211). Duration of use before onset (179): 1 year or less 25.1%, 2-5 years 36.3%, 6-10 years 16.8%, 11 years or more 21.8%. Median ages: first use 16 (IQR 14-18; 84), onset 24 (19-29; 101), diagnosis 28 (22-34; 111). Mean delay to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6). Follow-up documented for 85 of 211 (40.2%).
